1. Find the magnitude of the component of the pulling force F along the inclined plane, $\mathrm{F}_{1}$.
2. Find the magnitude of the normal force $\mathrm{F}_{\mathrm{N}}$ exerted by the box on the inclined plane.
3. Find the frictional force $\mathrm{F}_{\mathrm{f}}$ acting on the box.

Gcos\alpha - Fsin\beta
Fcos\beta - Gsin\alpha, direction along the incline downward

method.method_draft: Use a free-body diagram in axes parallel and perpendicular to the inclined plane. First describe the image: a block rests on an incline of angle α, and the applied force F is drawn above the plane making angle β with a dashed line parallel to the incline. From the text, the block moves upward at constant velocity, so acceleration is zero in both axes, and friction acts down the incline. Resolve F into F cos β along the plane and F sin β away from the plane; resolve weight G into G sin α down the plane and G cos α into the plane. Then F1 = F cos β. Perpendicular equilibrium gives the plane-on-block normal N = G cos α − F sin β, so the normal force exerted by the box on the plane has the same magnitude. Parallel equilibrium gives F cos β − G sin α − Ff = 0, hence Ff = F cos β − G sin α, directed down the incline.

3. 沿斜面方向平衡：F cos β - G sin α - F_f = 0，所以 F_f = F cos β - G sin α，方向沿斜面向下。

method.method_draft: Use projection plus work/energy for the along-plane balance. First describe the image: the dashed reference line through the point of application is parallel to the incline, and β is the angle from that line to the pulling force F; α is the ramp angle with the horizontal. Therefore the projection of the pull along the displacement direction is F1 = F cos β. Since the box slides upward at constant speed, the net work over any displacement s along the plane is zero. Over distance s, the pulling force does positive work F cos β · s; gravity does negative work G sin α · s; friction does negative work Ff · s because motion is upward and friction is downward. Setting total work to zero gives F cos β s − G sin α s − Ff s = 0, so Ff = F cos β − G sin α, down the incline. Separately, because there is no motion or acceleration normal to the plane, the outward normal component of the pull F sin β reduces the contact force, while the inward component of weight is G cos α; hence FN = G cos α − F sin β in magnitude for the force exerted by the box on the plane.

A pulling force F is applied to the box, directed upward at an angle above the inclined surface. A dashed reference line through the force application point is parallel to the incline, and the angle between this dashed line and F is labeled β.

Reasoning: Since β is measured from the direction parallel to the inclined plane to the pulling force F, the component of F along the plane is F1 = F cos β. The box moves upward along the incline at constant velocity, so the net work over any displacement s along the plane is zero. Along the plane, the pulling force does positive work F cos β · s. Gravity has a component G sin α down the plane, so it does negative work G sin α · s. Friction acts opposite the upward motion, so it is down the plane and does negative work Ff · s. Thus F cos β · s - G sin α · s - Ff · s = 0, giving Ff = F cos β - G sin α, directed down the incline. Perpendicular to the plane, there is no acceleration. The weight presses into the plane with component G cos α, while the outward perpendicular component of the pull is F sin β, reducing the contact force. Therefore the normal force magnitude is FN = G cos α - F sin β.

ready3_open_rewrite.resolved_question_text: A wooden box with a weight of $G$ is placed on a rough inclined plane with an inclination angle of $\alpha$. A constant force of magnitude $F$, directed at an angle $\beta$ above the inclined plane, is applied to pull the box upward. The box slides up the inclined plane at a constant velocity. 1. Find the magnitude of the component of the pulling force $F$ along the inclined plane, $\mathrm{F}_1$. 2. Find the magnitude of the normal force $\mathrm{F}_{\mathrm{N}}$ exerted by the box on the inclined plane. 3. Find the frictional force $\mathrm{F}_{\mathrm{f}}$ acting on the box.
ready3_open_rewrite.resolved_answer: 1. $F\cos\beta$ 2. $G\cos\alpha - F\sin\beta$ 3. $F\cos\beta - G\sin\alpha$, direction along the incline downward
ready3_open_rewrite.final_cot:
Image description: In the attached figure, a wooden box is placed on an inclined plane slanting upward to the right, and the angle between the inclined plane and the horizontal plane is labeled α. Above the wooden box there is a pulling force F, directed obliquely upward to the right; the figure also draws a dashed line parallel to the inclined plane, and the angle between the pulling force F and this dashed line parallel to the inclined plane is labeled β.

Reasoning: Take the coordinate axes along the direction of the inclined plane and perpendicular to the inclined plane. The wooden box moves uniformly upward along the inclined plane, so the acceleration is 0, and the resultant force in each direction is 0. The component of the pulling force F upward along the inclined plane is F cos β, and the component outward perpendicular to the inclined plane is F sin β. The component of gravity G downward along the inclined plane is G sin α, and the component inward perpendicular to the inclined plane is G cos α. Since the wooden box slides upward, the direction of the friction force is downward along the inclined plane.

1. The pulling-force component along the inclined plane is F1 = F cos β.
2. Equilibrium in the direction perpendicular to the inclined plane: N + F sin β = G cos α, so the supporting force of the inclined plane on the wooden box is N = G cos α - F sin β. The magnitude of the pressure of the wooden box on the inclined plane is equal to this, therefore F_N = G cos α - F sin β.
3. Equilibrium along the inclined plane: F cos β - G sin α - F_f = 0, so F_f = F cos β - G sin α, directed downward along the inclined plane.
